Trapeziometacarpal Joint Osteoarthritis
 CORE
June 30, 2025
Julie Adams, MD (2020–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
List tools for the diagnosis and evaluation of trapeziometacarpal joint osteoarthritis.
Discuss treatment options for trapeziometacarpal joint osteoarthritis.
Describe factors that influence treatment options or may lead to the use of adjunctive
measures.
Epidemiology
Overview
The incidence of primary osteoarthritis of the thumb carpometacarpal (CMC;
trapeziometacarpal [TMC]) joint increases with age.
The incidence of individuals seeking care for TMC joint osteoarthritis is higher in women, which
may reflect societal norms for seeking medical care.

Pseudo–population-based studies suggest radiographic evidence of TMC joint osteoarthritis is
an expected aspect of normal human aging in men and women.1
The high prevalence of TMC joint osteoarthritis suggests that most individuals accommodate
the condition, which is supported by other lines of evidence.2,3
Risk Factors
Increasing age
Likely genetic factors

Risk Factors
Care for TMC joint osteoarthritis is more common in women than men; however,
radiographic incidence is universal with age in both sexes. Evidence from multiple lines
of inquiry suggests that TMC joint osteoarthritis generally is accommodated. Individuals
who present for treatment may accommodate symptoms over time.1,4,5
Pathophysiology
Pathoanatomy
The TMC joint is a biconcave saddle-shaped joint with a high degree of freedom (Figure 1).
This shape confers substantial multiplanar motion with little bony constraint.
The joint is stabilized by a complex set of capsuloligamentous structures6 (Figure 2).
The most important stabilizers appear to be the anterior oblique ligament (volar beak
ligament) and the dorsoradial ligament.

joint. Minimal bone congruity allows for thumb carpometacarpal motion, which includes
extension, flexion, adduction, and abduction. These four movements can be combined to form
the complex movements of opposition and retropulsion, palmar abduction, radial abduction,
palmar adduction, and radial adduction. (Adapted with permission from Ateshian GA,
Rosenwasser MP, Mow VC: Curvature characteristics and congruence of the thumb
carpometacarpal joint: Differences between female and male joints. J Biomech 1992;25[6]:591-
607.)

posterior oblique ligament (POL), dorsoradial ligament (DRL), abductor pollicis longus (APL), first
intermetacarpal ligament (IML), and extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL) tendon. B, Palmar view
shows the anterior oblique ligament (AOL), ulnar collateral ligament (UCL), first IML, APL tendon,

= second metacarpal, MIII = third metacarpal. (Reproduced with permission from Imaeda T, An
KN, Cooney WP III: Functional anatomy and biomechanics of the thumb. Hand Clin 1992;8[1]:9-
15.)

TMC Joint
Patients with ligamentous laxity (within the spectrum of normal or with specific
pathology such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or lupus) may be more prone to
osteoarthritis or symptoms of osteoarthritis; however, this theory currently is not
supported by experimental evidence and may be in opposition to population-based
epidemiological studies.1,4,5 This has led to investigation of relaxin receptors, which are
related to pregnancy-associated pelvic laxity in women and are found in the capsule of

the TMC joint.7 This may account for the relative prevalence of women seeking
treatment.
Symptoms
Pain occurs at the base of the thumb, particularly during actions that generate force across the
joint, such as pinch and grip.
Patients may note fullness at the base of the thumb.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Physical Examination
The joint is tender.
Pain and crepitus with axial pressure and circumduction of the TMC joint (the so-called grind
test) suggest advanced osteoarthritis (Video 1).
Passive dorsoradial subluxation of the TMC joint (ballottement test) often elicits pain.
Patients may note thumb deformity.
The thumb metacarpal joint can subluxate dorsally and radially on the trapezium, creating a
bump, which occasionally is referred to as a shoulder sign.
Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint hyperextension may occur in combination with metacarpal
adduction (Figure 3).

Differential Diagnosis
de Quervain tenosynovitis
Scaphotrapeziotrapezoid (STT) osteoarthritis
Scaphoid nonunion
Radioscaphoid arthritis
Carpal tunnel syndrome (symptoms do not overlap; common misdiagnosis by non-specialists)
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
Typically three radiographic views of the wrist are obtained, with or without a Robert
radiograph of the thumb (joint-specific radiograph with the x-ray beam centered on the
TMC joint and the dorsal aspect of the thumb flat on the cassette (hyper-pronated—a
true AP view of the thumb; the x-ray beam is oriented 15° proximal to vertical)8 (Figure
4). This hyperpronated view allows for visualization of all the joint articulations with the
trapezium. Alternatively, a Bett or Gedda radiograph is a PA view of the thumb in which
all articulations are visualized (Figure 5). Using a Robert radiograph alone for staging
may be associated with higher interobserver and intraobserver reliability with regard to
staging of thumb TMC joint osteoarthritis.8,9
Lateral radiographs and radiographs including the wrist are important to obtain to
evaluate for concomitant carpal malalignment, which may affect treatment options.

Classification
Staging does not correlate with symptoms but is commonly used.
The Eaton staging system is the most used staging system (Figure 6).
Stage I: radiographs normal or slight widening from synovitis
Stage II: narrowing and small osteophytes at the TMC joint
Stage III: narrowing and large osteophytes at the TMC joint
Stage IV: involvement of the STT joint
Figure 6 Bett radiographs of the thumb carpometacarpal (CMC) joint and the scaphotrapezial
joint demonstrate the Eaton staging system for thumb CMC arthritis. A, Eaton stage I thumb CMC
arthritis, with normal articular cartilage and a widened joint space. B, Eaton stage II thumb CMC
arthritis. Note the slight narrowing at the thumb CMC joint space (<2 mm) along with maintained
joint contours, minimal sclerosis, and joint debris. Lateral dorsal subluxation of the thumb
metacarpal on the trapezium is observed on this radiograph; however, this is variably present in
patients with stage II disease. C, Eaton stage III thumb CMC arthritis. Note the considerable
narrowing of the thumb CMC joint space along with sclerosis, cyst formation, and osteophytes
(>2 mm in length). Joint subluxation usually is present and is observed on this radiograph. D,
Eaton stage IV thumb CMC osteoarthritis. Note the considerable thumb CMC joint space

Nonsurgical Management
Accommodation is a useful health strategy and one that surgeons are ethically
obligated to suggest to patients
Identification and reorientation of common misconceptions
Alleviation of distress
Maintenance of evolution of roles
Palliative management (symptom alleviation)
Splinting
Use of adaptative equipment
Intrinsic muscle strengthening
Only non-controlled, non-experimental support to date
Non-opioid analgesia
Steroid and other injections
Transient relief at best
Not clearly better than a placebo

Nonsurgical Management
Patients should be educated that symptoms may be managed nonsurgically and are not
worrisome or dangerous. Patients who continue nonsurgical treatment are not missing
an opportunity for intervention. Patients also should be reminded that radiographic
staging does not correlate with symptoms. In many patients, radiographic findings of
osteoarthritis are apparent but symptoms are absent. In addition, many patients find
that their symptoms resolve or dissipate over time without any specific treatment.
Some patients may find that awareness of symptoms associated with activity is helpful;
however, they should understand that symptoms may be worse after an activity, such as
gardening, and that they are not creating additional damage. Surgeons should reassure
patients that symptoms likely will regress to the mean after a short period of
exacerbation.

In some patients, brace or splint immobilization or the use of other such supports may
provide some relief. No universal agreement nor evidence supports the use of custom-
molded splints versus off-the-shelf splints or long versus short opponens splints
(forearm-based versus hand-based splints); some studies question whether a thumb
spica component is helpful.10 Most commonly, patients will consider a forearm-based or
hand-based thumb spica splint with the thumb interphalangeal joint free; however,
patients should be encouraged to consider various options and, with trial and error, find
the option that appears to best ameliorate symptoms.
Many patients find the use of a sleeve or a compressive wrap about the thumb to be
supportive., Similar to splint or brace immobilization, the use of a sleeve or a
compressive wrap does not change the natural history of the condition but may
decrease symptoms or serve as a reminder to limit grip or pinch on that site.
Physical or occupational therapists can help with some palliative measures if desired.
Physical or occupational therapists can direct patients to adaptive equipment and tools,
such as wrapping tape about a pen or pencil so it is fatter and less painful to pinch.
Physical or occupational therapists may fabricate splints or mold splints for patients;
however, evidence suggests these are no better than off-the-shelf splints.10-15 Physical
or occupational therapists also can teach patients muscle strengthening exercises.16-19
Surgical Management
Can be offered to patients not satisfied with accommodation and palliative treatment
Some studies suggest the percentage of patients who elect to undergo surgical treatment is
low.1
Notable surgeon-to-surgeon variation exists.
Surgeons should take care to not impose their values on patients and ensure patients are
making decisions based on the factors that matter most to them (their values) rather than
misconceptions or false hope.
Various surgical treatment options are available for the management of thumb CMC joint
osteoarthritis.
SEND FEEDBACK


Surgical Management
Available evidence shows that simple trapeziectomy alone is necessary and sufficient for
amelioration of symptoms if surgical management is performed; additional procedures
result in a higher complication rate, increased surgical time, and increased costs without
improved outcomes.20-24 Regardless, variations and alternatives have been proposed
and are commonly performed. Postoperative complications include subsidence and
impingement of the thumb metacarpal on the distal scaphoid, which may result in
shortening of the thumb axis with weakness and recurrent/new pain. Therefore, various
alternative or adjunct procedures have been proposed. Although these complications
are rare, surgical procedures that purport or are designed to decrease these
complications are common; only 6% of procedures performed at the CMC joint are
simple trapeziectomy.
Techniques/Procedures
Trapeziectomy with interposition
Commonly, the palmaris longus is harvested, rolled up, and interposed into the post-
trapeziectomy defect.
Occasionally, this is called an anchovy procedure and may be performed in combination
with other stabilization type procedures.
No evidence suggests that this improves outcomes after thumb CMC joint surgery.
Various other materials have been interposed, including allogenic skin, other autogenic
tendon grafts, collagen sponges (such as gel foam), and manufactured materials.
No evidence shows that this improves outcomes after thumb CMC joint surgery.
Pinning or other stabilization
So called hematoma distraction arthroplasty is a simple trapeziectomy with temporary
pinning of the post-trapeziectomy space, usually for 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively.
This allows for scarring, such that the post-trapeziectomy space is maintained.
This treatment option is used more rarely because of pin-associated complications and
pain.
No evidence shows that this improves outcomes after thumb CMC joint surgery.
The use of suture button suspension devices is an alternative to pinning.

Proponents suggest that this may allow for earlier rehabilitation or less immobilization;
however, robust data are lacking.
Complications include bothersome prominence of the buttons on the thumb metacarpal
and the index metacarpal, impingement or stiffness from over-tightening the construct,
and fracture of the first and or second metacarpal.
No evidence suggests that this improves outcomes after thumb CMC joint surgery.
Ligament reconstruction, tendon transfers, or suspensionplasty with or without tendon
interposition
All or part of the flexor carpi radialis (FCR) may be harvested and routed about itself or the
abductor pollicis longus (APL) or through drill holes in the first or second metacarpal to
suspend the thumb or reconstruct the ligaments.
Tendon interposition may or may not be used.
Common techniques include the following:
Using all or part of the FCR and routing it about itself or the APL
Using a slip of the APL and routing it through the thumb metacarpal or about the FCR
Using suture with or without a suture anchor to coapt the APL to the FCR (so-called suture
suspensionplasty).
No evidence shows that this improves outcomes after thumb TMC joint surgery (Resource 1).
Arthroscopy
Arthroscopy has been proposed for the management of thumb CMC joint osteoarthritis.
Typically two portals are used, and procedures vary from capsular shrinkage (heating of the
capsule to tighten the ligaments) to partial or complete resection of the trapezium with or
without interposition of materials.
Reported outcomes are similar to those of other procedures about the thumb CMC joint, with
no evidence showing that interposition improves outcomes and evidence suggesting that
patients with stage IV disease do not have poorer outcomes after partial trapeziectomy than
patients with osteoarthritis not involving the STT joint.20
Potential complications include thermal burns and other complications common with
procedures for the management of thumb CMC joint osteoarthritis, including superficial radial
neuritis; persistent or recurrent pain; and/or injury to normal structures, including the radial
artery or tendons.
Arthroplasty or Implants

Implant arthroplasty or joint arthroplasty is an uncommonly performed procedure for the
management of thumb CMC joint osteoarthritis.
In the past, implants have been plagued by mechanical failure, instability, or persistent pain.
Currently, little evidence exists to support their use.
Thumb CMC Joint Fusion
Thumb CMC joint fusion also is an uncommon procedure, performed by approximately 6% of
hand surgeons. It is most commonly performed in young patients, young patients with
posttraumatic arthritis, patients with an unstable thumb or ligamentous laxity, and younger,
high-demand laborers with basilar arthritis.
Thumb CMC joint fusion may be performed by osteotomizing the proximal end of the thumb
metacarpal and the trapezium or, more commonly, via a cup-and-cone technique with the use
of a burr to prepare the bony surfaces. Bone graft is applied, and compression and fixation are
achieved with the use of screws, Kirschner wires, tension band, or plate and screw fixation.
The thumb is placed in a position of palmar and radial abduction; an intraoperative evaluation
is performed to ensure the thumb can be passively opposed to the radial aspect of the index
middle phalanx, which ensures appropriate positioning.
Common complications include hardware irritation and the expectation that arthritis of the
STT joint will occur over time.
Patients should be advised that they will have difficulty placing the thumb in the plane of the
palm of the hand and, therefore, will have trouble getting the hand flat into tight spaces, which
may be problematic for plumbers or electricians.
Nonunion is not infrequent but often is asymptomatic.
If symptomatic STT arthritis occurs after thumb CMC joint fusion, the fusion may be taken
down and osteotomized for a trapeziectomy with anticipated good results.
Special Cases
Young patients with Eaton stage I osteoarthritis or with traumatic instability.
These patients often have joint subluxation, which is believed to contribute to symptoms and,
eventually, arthritis. These patients may be amenable to ligament reconstruction (without
trapeziectomy) with the use of a portion of the FCR to re-create the thumb CMC ligaments.
Other proposed treatment options include arthrotomy and tightening of the dorsoradial
capsule.

14/19

Patients with globalized ligament laxity or early joint cartilage damage may be best treated via
thumb CMC joint fusion.
Patients with MCP joint hyperextension
Compensatory thumb MCP joint hyperextension may develop over time. Discussion with
regard to the implications of this deformity on surgical management is ongoing.
Several good long-term studies suggest no difference in the outcomes of patients who
undergo treatment and patients who do not undergo treatment for thumb MCP joint
hyperextension during thumb CMC joint surgery.6,22
Other studies suggest that the zigzag collapse of the thumb, if unmanaged, results in
excessive forces on the thumb CMC joint surgical site, causing progressive collapse,
subsidence, and pain at the thumb CMC joint site.25,26
Many surgeons use a stepwise approach for thumb MCP joint compensatory hyperextension.
If hyperextension is 30° or less, no treatment is performed.
If hyperextension is greater than 30°, MCP joint pinning, capsular advancement of the volar
plate, sesamoidectomy, or MCP joint fusion may be considered.
If patients have an unstable MCP joint (radial-ulnar instability) or arthritis, MCP joint fusion
is favored.
